reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant multisystem disorder caused chiefly by pathogenic variants in JAG1, and less often NOTCH2, disrupting Notch signalling during development
The hepatic hallmark is paucity of the interlobular bile ducts on liver biopsy, producing chronic cholestasis, pruritus, and xanthomata
Cardiac involvement is common, classically peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, and tetralogy of Fallot is the most frequent complex lesion
Characteristic facies include a broad forehead, deep-set eyes, a pointed chin, and a bulbous nasal tip, giving an inverted-triangle appearance
Ocular posterior embryotoxon and skeletal butterfly vertebrae are supportive diagnostic features
Renal disease and vascular anomalies, including intracranial aneurysms, contribute to morbidity and sudden events

Management is supportive with treatment of pruritus (including ileal bile acid transport inhibitors), nutritional and fat-soluble vitamin support, and liver transplantation in decompensated cholestasis
reference.pathophysiology: Alagille syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of the Notch signalling pathway, most commonly through mutations in the ligand JAG1 and occasionally the receptor NOTCH2. Notch signalling is essential for the differentiation and branching morphogenesis of intrahepatic bile ducts, as well as for cardiac, vascular, renal, skeletal, and ocular development. Impaired signalling leads to progressive loss (paucity) of the interlobular bile ducts, causing chronic intrahepatic cholestasis with retention of bile acids and cholesterol, alongside the syndrome's characteristic extrahepatic malformations. Expressivity is highly variable even within families.
additionalDifferentials: Other syndromic causes of ductal paucity
additionalInvestigations: Liver biopsy demonstrating bile duct paucity
Molecular genetic testing of JAG1 and NOTCH2
Echocardiography and cardiac imaging for pulmonary artery and structural anomalies
Ophthalmological slit-lamp examination for posterior embryotoxon
Renal ultrasound and function tests, with vascular imaging where clinically indicated
redFlags: Severe congenital heart disease causing cyanosis or heart failure
Sudden neurological deterioration from an intracranial vascular event
Progressive cholestatic liver failure with coagulopathy
Intractable pruritus with disabling quality-of-life impact
reference.prognosis: Outcome is largely determined by the severity of cardiac and vascular anomalies and the progression of liver disease; many patients do well, but a subset develops end-stage cholestatic liver disease requiring transplantation, and vascular events can cause sudden morbidity or mortality.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing infants as biliary atresia and proceeding to unnecessary Kasai portoenterostomy
Underestimating vascular risk, including intracranial aneurysms and bleeding
Assuming absence of the classic facies or one feature excludes the diagnosis given variable expressivity
Neglecting cardiac assessment before considering liver transplantation
Failing to counsel on the autosomal dominant inheritance and variable family expression
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
management: Manage cholestatic pruritus with the ileal bile acid transport inhibitor maralixibat, alongside agents such as rifampicin, ursodeoxycholic acid, colestyramine or naltrexone
Nutritional support with high-energy feeds and supplementation of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K
Surveillance and treatment of chronic cholestasis complications including xanthomata, fractures and growth failure
Cardiology assessment and management of associated lesions such as peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis or tetralogy of Fallot
Monitor for progression to end-stage liver disease with consideration of biliary diversion for intractable pruritus and liver transplantation
Vascular surveillance for intracranial aneurysms and renal assessment for associated nephropathy
Multidisciplinary care spanning hepatology, cardiology, ophthalmology and clinical genetics
Genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant condition with testing of at-risk relatives given variable expressivity
